question: What do we call a normal, smooth, and uncomplicated labour and delivery?
explanation: You've got this! Eutocia is just the medical word for a normal, straightforward delivery, while dystocia means a difficult labour. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: A pregnancy is considered a normal term birth when delivery happens during which window?

options.C: Breech presentation with a single fetus

explanation: Spot on! A full-term pregnancy that is ready for normal labour usually falls between 37 and 42 completed weeks with one baby in a head-down position. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: When does the first stage of labour officially come to an end?

options.C: When the cervix is completely dilated
options.D: When the baby is fully born

explanation: Well done! The first stage runs from the start of regular contractions all the way until the cervix is fully open at 10 cm. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: What major event marks the exact beginning of the third stage of labour?
explanation: Great thinking! The moment the baby is safely out, the third stage kicks off—and it wraps up once the placenta is delivered too. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: Why do midwives and nurses perform Leopold's maneuvers when a mother is admitted?

options.A: To assess fetal lie, presentation, and position
options.B: To check for signs of a postpartum infection
options.C: To measure cervical dilation in centimeters
options.D: To determine the exact gestational age in weeks

explanation: You're doing great! Leopold's maneuvers are simply systematic hand movements on the tummy to figure out how the baby is lying before doing an internal check. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: A pregnant woman comes in with painless bleeding late in her pregnancy. Which action should you definitely avoid?

options.A: Listening to the fetal heart rate

explanation: Smart choice! If you suspect placenta praevia because of painless bleeding, putting fingers inside for an exam can trigger severe, life-threatening bleeding. Safety first! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: During the active phase of the first stage of labour, how often should you listen to the baby's heart rate?
explanation: Keep it up! Checking the fetal heart rate every 30 minutes helps you catch any signs of distress early and keep both mom and baby safe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: Why is it important to encourage a labouring mum to empty her bladder regularly?

options.A: To speed up cervical dilation past 10 centimeters
options.B: To stop Braxton Hicks contractions from returning
options.C: To prevent the bladder from obstructing fetal descent
options.D: To collect urine for a daily routine glucose test

explanation: Brilliant! A full bladder gets in the way like a water balloon in the pelvis, which can slow down the baby's journey down the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: At what point does the second stage of labour officially start?

options.B: When the cervix is completely dilated
options.D: When contractions become painful and regular

explanation: You nailed it! The second stage begins right when the cervix is fully open at 10 cm and ends when the baby is born. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: Why do we carefully control the speed at which the baby's head is born?

options.A: To ensure the placenta detaches immediately
options.B: To prevent the umbilical cord from snapping
options.C: To give the mother time to drink water
options.D: To prevent severe tearing of the perineum

explanation: Spot on! Guiding the head out slowly gives the perineal tissues time to stretch gently, preventing deep tears. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: What is the main medication given during Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL)?
explanation: You've got this! Oxytocin is our go-to medication because it works fast to help the womb contract safely after delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard step in AMTSL?

options.A: Controlled traction on the umbilical cord
options.C: Routine manual removal of the placenta
options.D: Massage of the uterine fundus after delivery

explanation: Great job! We never pull the placenta out by hand routinely—that's only done if it fails to come out naturally with gentle cord traction. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: In the very first hour after delivery (the fourth stage), how often should you check the mother's vital signs and womb tone?
explanation: Keep shining! Because the risk of bleeding is highest right after birth, we monitor her closely every 15 minutes during that first hour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: You feel a new mother's uterus and notice it feels soft, boggy, and pushed to the right. What should you do right away?

options.A: Prepare the patient for immediate surgery
options.B: Administer a dose of oral iron tablets
options.C: Encourage the mother to empty her bladder
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back

explanation: Wonderful clinical thinking! A full bladder often pushes the womb out of place and stops it from tightening up. Once she pees, the womb usually firms right back up! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilation does the alert line begin on a standard WHO partograph?
explanation: You're doing amazing! The partograph alert line starts ticking once active labour gets going at 4 cm dilation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)

question: What must you do if a labouring woman's progress on the partograph crosses over the action line?

options.A: Take immediate steps for intervention and management
options.B: Discharge the patient home for rest
options.C: Wait another four hours without changes
options.D: Switch from monitoring vitals to once daily

explanation: Spot on! Crossing the action line is a clear warning sign that labour isn't going as smoothly as expected, so prompt medical action is required to help mother and baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)
